# Renoxium: the developer documentation in one file

> Renoxium is a multi-tenant hosting platform for web applications and functions written in TypeScript. An app is TypeScript functions and HTML pages in folders that are its routes; it runs in a V8 isolate with its own SQLite file, under CPU, memory, wall-clock and network limits enforced by the platform, and it assembles auth, organisations, billing, admin, storage, email and other official modules instead of writing them. The toolkit a developer types is `renox`: the CLI (`renox new`, `dev`, `check`, `test`, `deploy`) and the npm package `@renoxium/sdk` (types, helpers, test fakes).

The documents below are the developer-facing ones of https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/blob/main/, in reading order, each introduced by a "Source:" line with its path and URL. Relative links inside a document are repository paths. The index is https://renoxium.com/llms.txt; the rendered pages are under https://renoxium.com/docs/.

---

Source: docs/getting-started.md (https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md)

# Getting started

From an empty folder to an app at `https://<app>.renoxium.app` in about ten minutes: install the CLI, create an app, run it locally, sign in, deploy. Each step shows what you should see. Every command is the real one from the [CLI reference](../cli/README.md).

## Prerequisites

- **Linux or macOS** (x64 or arm64). **Windows:** use WSL 2 with Ubuntu (`wsl --install -d Ubuntu` in PowerShell, then run every command below inside the Ubuntu terminal).
- **[Bun](https://bun.sh) 1.4 or newer** for `bun install` and `renox test`: `curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash`, then open a new terminal. `bun --version` prints `1.4.x` or newer.
- `curl`, and a browser for the sign-in.

## Install

One line installs `renox`, and the `renox-worker` it runs your app on locally, into `~/.renox/bin`. It installs a file only when its SHA-256 matches the release:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/releases/download/cli-v0.1.4/install.sh | sh
```

If the installer says `~/.renox/bin` is not on your `PATH`, add it (and add the same line to `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc`):

```sh
export PATH="$HOME/.renox/bin:$PATH"
```

Check it:

```sh
renox --version
```

```
renox 0.1.3 (renox-worker 0.3.0)
```

There is no npm package for the CLI: `npx renox` and `bunx renox` do not work. The SDK your app imports is the npm package `@renoxium/sdk`. Verifying the signatures and upgrading are in [Developer experience](12-developer-experience.md#installing-the-cli).

## Your first app

```sh
renox new my-app --template hello
```

```
Created my-app/. Next:

  cd my-app
  bun install        # the @renoxium/sdk types and test helpers
  renox dev          # http://localhost:8787, reloads on save
  renox login        # once: approve the sign-in in the dashboard
  renox deploy       # prints the live URL

Docs: https://renoxium.com/docs
```

`hello` writes a function (`functions/api/hello.ts`), a home page (`pages/index.html` and its layout), a test (`tests/hello.test.ts`), `renox.toml`, `package.json`, `tsconfig.json`, a `README.md` and the files for coding agents (`AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.mcp.json`). `--template blank` writes one health route and nothing else.

```sh
cd my-app
bun install
```

```
+ bun-types@1.4.4
+ typescript@7.0.2
+ @renoxium/sdk@0.1.3

6 packages installed
```

`typescript` is what `renox check` type checks your code with.

Run it:

```sh
renox dev
```

```
renox dev: http://localhost:8787  (artifact 982e73345217, 2 routes)
  GET     /api/hello
  PAGE    /
```

Open `http://localhost:8787`: the page says "my-app is running". `http://localhost:8787/api/hello` answers `{"ok":true}`. Edit `pages/index.html` or the function and save: the browser reloads. Stop it with Ctrl-C.

Folders are routes: `functions/api/hello.ts` answers `/api/hello`, `pages/products/[id].html` is the page at `/products/:id` with its loader in `pages/products/[id].ts`. The model is in [App model](07-app-model.md).

## Check and test

```sh
renox check
```

```
renox check: ok
```

```sh
renox test
```

```
 2 pass
 0 fail
```

`renox check` validates the configuration, the routes and templates, lints SQL and scans for secrets. `renox test` runs `tests/*.test.ts` on the same local worker as `renox dev`, with a fresh database for each test file.

## Sign in

Create an account at `https://dashboard.renoxium.com/signup` (email, a password of at least 12 characters, a workspace id) and open the link in the email: the dashboard signs you in. Then, in the app folder:

```sh
renox login
```

```
Open https://dashboard.renoxium.com/device?code=BCDF-GHJK
and check that it shows the code BCDF-GHJK, then approve.
Waiting for approval…
Signed in to my-workspace. Token saved to /home/you/.config/renox/credentials.json
```

The link opens the dashboard's device page with the code filled in: check that the code matches, keep or narrow the scopes, and press Approve. The token is kept in `~/.config/renox/credentials.json` (readable only by you) for 90 days. In CI, set `RENOX_TOKEN` to a token from the dashboard's Tokens page instead.

## Deploy

```sh
renox deploy
```

```
Bundling… 2 routes, 1 modules, 2 templates               0.2s
  Created app my-app
  Uploading 0.0 MB → api.renoxium.com                      0.0s
  Validating… ✓ manifest ✓ routes ✓ templates ✓ permissions ✓ bundle (validated)
  Activating… ✓ migrations ✓ cell ✓ probe                  0.1s
  Live: https://my-app.renoxium.app  (10db4d689fa2)        total 0.6s
```

`renox deploy` first type checks the app (as `renox check` does) and stops on a type error. The next deploy also prints `Rollback: renox deploy --rollback <previous hash>`.

The first deploy creates the app under the name in `renox.toml`; the app names are global, so pick another name in `renox.toml` if it is taken. Every deploy is kept: `renox deploy --rollback` switches back to the previous one without a build or an upload. Then:

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `renox logs --follow` | The app's log lines as they happen |
| `printf %s "$VALUE" \| renox secrets set NAME` | A secret, read from stdin and never from an argument |
| `renox add auth` | Installs a module (and the official modules it needs) after showing its permissions ([Modules](10-modules.md)) |
| `renox db export` | A snapshot of the app's SQLite database ([Data](06-data.md)) |
| `renox <command> --help` | The options of any command |

## What next

- [App model](07-app-model.md): pages, loaders and actions, functions, webhooks, jobs, the `ctx` surface.
- [Templates](08-template-engine.md): HTML-first templates with `r-*` attributes.
- [Modules](10-modules.md): sign-in, organisations, billing and admin as installed modules.
- [Limits](contracts/ops.md#10-limits-per-tier-and-behaviour-on-limit): what the platform enforces per request and per app.
- [AI agents and MCP](20-ai-agents-mcp.md): `renox mcp` for coding agents.

To work on the platform itself from a clone of the repository instead: `git clone https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs && cd renox.rs && bun install && bun cli/scripts/fetch-worker.ts`, then run the CLI as `bun cli/src/main.ts`.

Source: docs/tutorial/README.md (https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/blob/main/docs/tutorial/README.md)

# Tutorial: build a team board

In about an hour you go from an empty folder to a multi-user app on `https://<app>.renoxium.app`. You build a small **team task board**: people sign up, create a team, invite each other, add and tick off tasks, and everyone on the team sees changes live. Only admins and owners remove tasks.

The app has no auth code of its own and no client framework. It uses pages and templates, one SQLite database, a few actions, two official modules, one Cedar policy file and a live feed. Each chapter adds one of these.

## Before you start

- Linux or macOS (Windows: WSL 2 with Ubuntu), [Bun](https://bun.sh) 1.4 or newer, `curl`, and a browser.
- TypeScript and HTML at the level of a form and a `fetch`. You do not need to know htmx, Cedar or SQLite: each is explained when it first appears.

## The chapters

| # | Chapter | What the board can do afterwards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [Install the CLI and create the app](01-install.md) | It runs locally: one page, one API route, one test |
| 2 | [The dev loop](02-dev-loop.md) | It has a stylesheet, and you have seen the error overlay |
| 3 | [Pages and templates](03-pages.md) | `/board` lists tasks through a layout, a partial and translated strings |
| 4 | [Data](04-data.md) | The tasks live in SQLite, created by a migration |
| 5 | [Functions and forms](05-actions.md) | You add, tick off and remove tasks; htmx swaps only the list |
| 6 | [Sign-in and teams with modules](06-teams.md) | People sign up, create teams and invite each other; each team has its own tasks |
| 7 | [Authorization](07-authorization.md) | A Cedar policy keeps every team's tasks to its members |
| 8 | [Realtime](08-realtime.md) | Every member sees changes without reloading |
| 9 | [Tests](09-tests.md) | A test flow for each role, with snapshots of what each one sees |
| 10 | [Deploy and a custom domain](10-deploy.md) | It is live, with logs, usage and your own domain |

## The checkpoints

Every chapter ends at a checkpoint: a complete app in [`examples/tutorial/`](../../examples/tutorial/) (`step-01` … `step-10`). If your copy stops working, compare it with the checkpoint, or continue from there:

```sh
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs
cp -r renox.rs/examples/tutorial/step-05 my-board
```

Each step contains the whole previous step plus that chapter's changes. The code blocks in the chapters are copied from the checkpoint files, and the repository's CI fails when one drifts (`cli/tests/tutorial.test.ts`). The same CI builds every checkpoint, runs `renox check` on it and passes its `renox test`.

## Building with an AI agent

Every app `renox new` writes includes `AGENTS.md` (the app model, the commands and the rules) and `.mcp.json`, which registers `renox mcp --project .` with Claude Code, Cursor and other agents. Each chapter ends with a short note on doing that chapter's step with an agent. How agents work with Renoxium: [AI agents and MCP](../20-ai-agents-mcp.md).

Source: docs/tutorial/01-install.md (https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/blob/main/docs/tutorial/01-install.md)

# Chapter 1: Install the CLI and create the app

**What you build:** the starting point of the board, an app with one page, one API route and one test, running on your machine.

## Install the CLI

One line installs `renox`, and the `renox-worker` it runs your app on, into `~/.renox/bin`. Each file is installed only if its SHA-256 matches the release:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/releases/download/cli-v0.1.4/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.renox/bin:$PATH"   # also add this line to ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc
renox --version
```

```
renox 0.1.4 (renox-worker 0.3.0)
```

The CLI is not on npm: `npx renox` and `bunx renox` do not work. The SDK your app imports is the npm package `@renoxium/sdk`. More on installing, verifying signatures and upgrading: [Getting started](../getting-started.md#install).

## Create the app

```sh
renox new my-board --template tutorial
cd my-board
bun install
```

`--template tutorial` writes this chapter's checkpoint. You can also copy it from the repository:

```sh
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs && cp -r renox.rs/examples/tutorial/step-01 my-board
```

Either way you get:

| Path | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `renox.toml` | The app's name, time zone and permissions |
| `functions/api/health.ts` | An API route: `GET /api/health` |
| `pages/index.html`, `pages/_layouts/main.html` | The home page and the layout around it |
| `tests/app.test.ts` | A test that `renox test` runs on the real worker |
| `package.json`, `tsconfig.json` | The SDK, TypeScript and the Bun types; `renox check` type checks with them |
| `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `.mcp.json` | For coding agents (see the end of this chapter) |

## The files

`renox.toml` names the app and says what it may reach. An empty `network` list means `fetch` cannot reach any host. Every name in `secrets` must be declared before `ctx.secrets` can read it:

`renox.toml`:
```toml
[app]
name = "board"
timezone = "Asia/Dubai"

[permissions]
# Outbound hosts for fetch, e.g. ["api.stripe.com"]; empty = no network.
network = []
# Secret names the app reads from ctx.secrets.
secrets = []
```

Every file under `functions/` is a route: its path is the URL, and each exported HTTP method handles that method. A handler gets `ctx` (the request, the app's database, `fetch`, secrets, the log) and returns a `Response`:

`functions/api/health.ts`:
```ts
// GET /api/health answers {"ok":true}: a route for uptime checks.
//
// Every file under functions/ is a route: its path is the URL, and each
// exported HTTP method (GET, POST, ...) handles that method.
import type { Handler } from "@renoxium/sdk";

export const GET: Handler = () => Response.json({ ok: true });
```

The board will be mostly pages, but an app made only of `.html` pages builds too (artifact 1.6). We keep the health route because chapter 10 points an uptime check at it.

A page is an `.html` file under `pages/`; `pages/index.html` is `/`. `<r-layout use="main">` wraps it in `pages/_layouts/main.html`, and the layout's `<slot />` is where the page goes:

`pages/index.html`:
```html
<r-layout use="main">
  <h1>Team board</h1>
  <p>Your app is running. This page is <code>pages/index.html</code>: change it and save.</p>
  <p>The API answers at <a href="/api/health"><code>/api/health</code></a>.</p>
</r-layout>
```

`pages/_layouts/main.html`:
```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title><slot name="title">Team board</slot></title>
</head>
<body>
  <main>
    <slot />
  </main>
</body>
</html>
```

## Run it

```sh
renox dev
```

```
renox dev: http://localhost:8787  (artifact 1296b55f326f, 2 routes)
  GET     /api/health
  PAGE    /
```

Open http://localhost:8787. [What you should see: the home page of the new app](screenshots/01-running.png).

## Test it

`renox test` builds the app, starts the same worker as `renox dev` with a fresh database for each test file, and runs `tests/*.test.ts` with Bun:

`tests/app.test.ts`:
```ts
// `renox test` runs this file on the local worker, with a fresh database.
import { describe, expect, test } from "bun:test";
import { app } from "@renoxium/sdk/test";

const t = await app();

describe("the app", () => {
  test("the home page renders", async () => {
    const res = await t.page("/");
    expect(res.status).toBe(200);
    expect(res.html).toContain("Team board");
  });

  test('GET /api/health answers {"ok":true}', async () => {
    const res = await t.request("GET", "/api/health");
    expect(res.json()).toEqual({ ok: true });
  });
});
```

```sh
renox test
```

```
 2 pass
 0 fail
```

The first lines of the test file make it run only under `renox test`. Your app does not need them. They are there because the Renoxium repository runs its own `bun test` over every file it holds, these checkpoints included (#479 removes them).

## If it does not work

| You see | Why, and what to do |
| --- | --- |
| `renox: command not found` | `~/.renox/bin` is not on your `PATH`: run the `export` line above, then open a new terminal |
| `port 8787 is in use` | Another `renox dev` is running. Stop it, or run `renox dev --port 8788` |
| `renox test` exits with code 3, "`bun` is not on PATH" | Install Bun 1.4 or newer and open a new terminal |
| `RENOX_CLI_WORKER_UNVERIFIED` | The worker binary does not match the release checksums. Run the installer again; do not copy a worker from elsewhere |
| `unknown template "tutorial"` | Your CLI is 0.1.2: copy `step-01` as shown above |

## Building with an AI agent

`.mcp.json` registers `renox mcp --project .` with Claude Code and Cursor. In the app folder, ask your agent: "Read AGENTS.md, then run the app's checks and tests with the renox MCP tools." It uses `run_check` and `run_tests`, and `dev_status` once `renox dev` runs. The tools and the rules agents follow: [AI agents and MCP](../20-ai-agents-mcp.md).

**Checkpoint:** [`examples/tutorial/step-01`](../../examples/tutorial/step-01/). Next: [the dev loop](02-dev-loop.md).

---

Source: docs/tutorial/02-dev-loop.md (https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/blob/main/docs/tutorial/02-dev-loop.md)

# Chapter 2: The dev loop

**What you build:** a stylesheet and a header for the board. On the way you learn what `renox dev` does when you save, and where errors show up, from the server and from the browser.

## Save, and the browser follows

Keep `renox dev` running in one terminal. Each time you save, it rebuilds the app, starts a fresh isolate on the same worker (your database stays open) and reloads the open pages. One edited file usually appears in the browser within a second.

Add a stylesheet. Files under `public/` are served as they are, outside your app's isolate and its CPU quota:

`public/app.css`:
```css
:root { color-scheme: light dark; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; line-height: 1.5; }
body { margin: 0 auto; max-width: 40rem; padding: 0 1rem 3rem; }
header { display: flex; gap: 1rem; align-items: center; flex-wrap: wrap; padding-block: 1rem; border-block-end: 1px solid #8884; }
a { color: inherit; }
```

Link it from the layout, and add a header:

`pages/_layouts/main.html`:
```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title><slot name="title">Team board</slot></title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/app.css">
</head>
<body>
  <header>
    <a href="/"><strong>Team board</strong></a>
  </header>
  <main>
    <slot />
  </main>
</body>
</html>
```

Save, and the page restyles itself. In the page source the link reads `/app.<hash>.css`, not `/app.css`. `renox build` adds a copy of the file named after its content and points the template at it, so browsers and Cloudflare can cache it until the file changes ([App model, static files](../07-app-model.md#static-files-public)).

## The error overlay

Break something on purpose. In `functions/api/health.ts`, delete the `)` before the last `;` and save. The build fails, the terminal prints the error, and the browser shows it over the page with the file, line, column and a hint.

[What you should see: the overlay with `Expected ")" but found ";"`](screenshots/02-overlay.png).

Put the `)` back and save: the overlay goes and the page reloads. A runtime error in a loader or an action works the same way: the terminal prints it with the original TypeScript line (source maps are in the bundle), and the page shows the error page with the request id.

## Browser errors in the terminal

Every page loads the platform's small client script, `/__renox/client.js`. It reports what goes wrong in the browser: a JavaScript exception, an htmx request that failed or found no target, a script the content security policy blocked. Under `renox dev` each report is printed next to the server's lines:

```
[browser] js.error pages/index.html:12:7 TypeError: tasks is undefined (01JBQ3Z7MA…)
```

The id at the end is the request id of the page. The overlay's **Browser** tab lists the same events, and next to them the server log of that request. You will use this from chapter 5, when htmx starts swapping fragments.

## Check before you commit

`renox check` runs what `renox deploy` runs first: the TypeScript type check, `renox.toml`, routes, templates, the SQL lint, secrets in the bundle and the other rules:

```sh
renox check
```

```
renox check: ok
```

## If it does not work

| You see | Why, and what to do |
| --- | --- |
| The page does not reload after a save | The page was opened before `renox dev` started, or from another port. Reload it once by hand |
| The stylesheet is not applied | The link must be a literal `href="/app.css"` for the hashed copy; check the file is under `public/`, not `pages/` |
| `renox check` prints `types not checked: add typescript` | Run `bun install` in the app folder; `package.json` lists `typescript` |
| A blocked inline `<script>` (a `securitypolicyviolation` event) | Pages send a strict content security policy. Put scripts in `public/` and link them, as chapter 8 does |

## Building with an AI agent

With `renox dev` running, an agent reads the same errors through the MCP tool `dev_errors` (server errors and `browserErrors`) and the app's state through `dev_status`. Ask it to "fix the error renox dev shows" and it reads them rather than guessing.

**Checkpoint:** [`examples/tutorial/step-02`](../../examples/tutorial/step-02/). Next: [pages and templates](03-pages.md).

---

Source: docs/tutorial/03-pages.md (https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/blob/main/docs/tutorial/03-pages.md)

# Chapter 3: Pages and templates

**What you build:** the `/board` page. A loader gives it a list of tasks, the template loops over them through a partial, and the strings come from a translation file. The tasks are a fixed list for now; chapter 4 moves them into the database.

## A page is two files

`pages/board/index.html` is the page at `/board`. Next to it, `pages/board/index.ts` may export `load`, which returns the template's data. Either file can stand alone: an `.html` with no loader renders without data, and a loader can return a `Response` (a redirect, JSON) instead of data ([App model, pages](../07-app-model.md#pages-ts-and-html-pairs-are-optional)).

The tasks, for now:

`lib/tasks.ts`:
```ts
// The board's tasks. For now a fixed list; chapter 4 moves them into SQLite.

export type Task = {
  id: number;
  title: string;
  done: number;
};

const SAMPLE: Task[] = [
  { id: 3, title: "Invite the team", done: 0 },
  { id: 2, title: "Write the first page", done: 0 },
  { id: 1, title: "Install the renox CLI", done: 1 },
];

/** The tasks, open ones first. */
export function listTasks(): Task[] {
  return [...SAMPLE].sort((a, b) => a.done - b.done || b.id - a.id);
}
```

The loader:

`pages/board/index.ts`:
```ts
// GET /board: the loader returns the template's data.
import { listTasks } from "../../lib/tasks";

export function load() {
  const tasks = listTasks();
  return {
    tasks: tasks.map((t) => ({ ...t, done: t.done === 1 })),
    open: tasks.filter((t) => t.done === 0).length,
  };
}
```

`lib/` is plain TypeScript: it is not a route, and pages and functions import from it.

## The template

`pages/board/index.html`:
```html
<r-layout use="main">
  <r-group slot="title"><r-t key="board.title" /></r-group>
  <h1><r-t key="board.title" /></h1>
  <section id="tasks" r-fragment="tasks">
    <p class="count"><r-t key="board.open" :n="open | number" /></p>
    <ul>
      <li r-for="task in tasks"><x-task :task="task" /></li>
      <li class="empty" r-empty="tasks"><r-t key="board.empty" /></li>
    </ul>
  </section>
</r-layout>
```

What each part does:

| Syntax | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `<r-layout use="main">` | Wraps the page in `pages/_layouts/main.html` |
| `<r-group slot="title">` | Fills the layout's `<slot name="title">`; `r-group` itself emits no element |
| `r-for="task in tasks"` | Repeats the element for each item |
| `r-empty="tasks"` | Shown instead when the list is empty |
| `r-fragment="tasks"` | Names a part of the page that can be rendered alone (chapter 5 uses it) |
| `<x-task :task="task" />` | Renders the partial `partials/task.html`; `:task` passes a value, not a string |
| `<r-t key="board.open" :n="open \| number" />` | A translated string, with `{n}` filled in; `\| number` formats the number for the locale |

The partial declares its props, so a typo in a caller is a build error and not an empty box:

`partials/task.html`:
```html
<r-props task="Task" />
<article :class="{ task: true, done: task.done }">
  <span class="check"><r-group r-if="task.done">✓</r-group><r-group r-else>○</r-group></span>
  <span class="title" dir="auto">{{ task.title | truncate(80) }}</span>
</article>
```

`:class="{ task: true, done: task.done }"` sets the classes whose value is true. `r-if` / `r-else` choose one of two elements. `{{ task.title | truncate(80) }}` prints the title, escaped, cut at 80 characters. Escaping is automatic: a title of `<b>hi</b>` shows those characters, and no markup reaches the page. `dir="auto"` lets a title in Arabic run right to left.

Templates are a small language on purpose: property access, comparisons, `&&`, `||`, `!`, `??` and filters, and no function calls. Anything that needs code goes in the loader ([Templates](../08-template-engine.md)).

## Strings in one place

`<r-t key="…">` looks the key up in `i18n/<locale>.json`. The app's own catalogue needs no module:

`i18n/en.json`:
```json
{
  "home": {
    "title": "Your team's board",
    "intro": "Add tasks, tick them off, and see your team's changes as they happen.",
    "open_board": "Open the board"
  },
  "board": {
    "title": "Board",
    "open": "{n} open",
    "empty": "Nothing to do yet."
  }
}
```

The home page and the layout's header now use keys too:

`pages/index.html`:
```html
<r-layout use="main">
  <h1><r-t key="home.title" /></h1>
  <p><r-t key="home.intro" /></p>
  <p><a href="/board"><r-t key="home.open_board" /></a></p>
</r-layout>
```

`pages/_layouts/main.html`:
```html
  <header>
    <a href="/"><strong>Team board</strong></a>
    <a href="/board"><r-t key="board.title" /></a>
  </header>
```

A second language is a second file (`i18n/ar.json`) with the same keys; the `i18n` module (chapter 6 installs it) picks the locale for each visitor.

## See it

Open http://localhost:8787/board. [What you should see: two open tasks above the done one](screenshots/03-board.png).

The test asks for the page and checks the order:

`tests/board.test.ts`:
```ts
describe("the board", () => {
  test("lists the tasks, open ones first", async () => {
    const page = await t.page("/board");
    expect(page.status).toBe(200);
    expect(page.html).toContain("2 open");
    expect(page.html.indexOf("Invite the team")).toBeLessThan(page.html.indexOf("Install the renox CLI"));
    expect(page.html).toContain('<article class="task done">');
  });
```

## If it does not work

| You see | Why, and what to do |
| --- | --- |
| ``unknown component `<x-tsk>`: expected partials/tsk.html`` | The partial's file name must match the tag: `<x-task>` is `partials/task.html` |
| `i18n-missing-key  <r-t key="board.emptyy"> has no en translation` | The key is not in `i18n/en.json` (or the JSON does not parse) |
| `RENOX_RENDER_LIMIT` | A template ran out of render fuel (a loop over a huge list). Limit the list in the loader |
| A `{{ }}` shows up literally | Interpolation is not processed inside `<script>` and `<style>`, by design |

## Building with an AI agent

Ask: "Add a page at /board that lists tasks from a loader, with a partial for one task." The agent can call `search_docs` for the template syntax and `run_check` to see the template errors before you open the browser.

**Checkpoint:** [`examples/tutorial/step-03`](../../examples/tutorial/step-03/). Next: [data](04-data.md).

---

Source: docs/tutorial/04-data.md (https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/blob/main/docs/tutorial/04-data.md)

# Chapter 4: Data

**What you build:** a table for the tasks, created by a migration, and a loader that reads it with a parameterised query.

## One SQLite database per app

Every app has its own SQLite database: one file, opened next to your app's code, and nothing to provision or connect to. Your code reaches it through `ctx.db`. It never sees a file path or a connection string. Every statement passes an authorizer: your app's tables start with `app__`, and each module may touch only its own prefix (`auth__`, `org__`, …) ([Data](../06-data.md)).

## A migration

A migration is a `.sql` file in `migrations/`. They run once each, in name order, and only forward: to change a table later you add a new file, never edit an old one (chapter 6 does exactly that).

`migrations/001_tasks.sql`:
```sql
-- The board's tasks. Every table of the app starts with app__.
create table app__tasks (
  id         integer primary key,
  title      text    not null,
  done       integer not null default 0,
  created_at integer not null
) strict;
```

`strict` makes SQLite check the column types. Save: `renox dev` applies the new migration when it rebuilds. In production `renox deploy` runs pending migrations before the new code takes traffic.

## Read it in the loader

The tasks module now takes the database. The query has a `?` placeholder and the value goes in a separate array:

`lib/tasks.ts`:
```ts
// The board's tasks: the queries the page runs, always with parameters
// (`?`), never with a value pasted into the SQL.
import type { DbStatements } from "@renoxium/sdk";

export type Task = {
  id: number;
  title: string;
  done: number;
};

/** The tasks, open ones first. */
export function listTasks(db: DbStatements): Promise<Task[]> {
  return db.query<Task>("select id, title, done from app__tasks order by done, id desc limit ?", [200]);
}
```

The loader receives `ctx` and passes `db` on. `LoaderContext` is the type of a loader's `ctx`:

`pages/board/index.ts`:
```ts
// GET /board: the loader reads the tasks from the app's SQLite database.
import type { LoaderContext } from "@renoxium/sdk";

import { listTasks } from "../../lib/tasks";

export async function load({ db }: LoaderContext) {
  const tasks = await listTasks(db);
  return {
    tasks: tasks.map((t) => ({ ...t, done: t.done === 1 })),
    open: tasks.filter((t) => t.done === 0).length,
  };
}
```

The template and the partial do not change: the rows have the same shape as the fixed list of chapter 3.

## Never build SQL from strings

`renox check` refuses SQL put together from values:

```ts
db.query(`select id from app__tasks where title = '${title}'`);
```

```
lib/bad.ts:2:61  error  sql-interpolation  db.query(): SQL built with template interpolation; pass values as ? parameters
```

Always write `db.query("… where title = ?", [title])`. One gap to know about: the rule does not yet see through a type argument, so `` db.query<Task>(`…${title}`) `` passes the check (#474). The rule is a lint; the habit is the protection.

## Sample rows for the tests

The dev board is empty: there is no form until the next chapter. `renox test` loads every `seeds/*.sql` file into each test file's fresh database after the migrations:

`seeds/tasks.sql`:
```sql
-- Sample tasks. `renox test` loads seeds/*.sql into each test's database.
insert into app__tasks (title, done, created_at) values
  ('Install the renox CLI', 1, 0),
  ('Write the first page', 0, 0),
  ('Invite the team', 0, 0);
```

`docs/06-data.md` lists `renox db seed` to load the same files into the dev database. That command does not exist yet (#480).

The test now also checks the table:

`tests/board.test.ts`:
```ts
  test("the rows come from the migration's table", () => {
    expect(t.db.query("select count(*) as n from app__tasks")).toEqual([{ n: 3 }]);
  });
```

`t.db.query` reads the test's database directly, for assertions.

## See it

Open http://localhost:8787/board. [What you should see: "0 open" and "Nothing to do yet."](screenshots/04-board.png), because the dev database has the table and no rows. `renox test` sees the three seeded tasks:

```sh
renox test
```

```
 4 pass
 0 fail
```

## If it does not work

The database codes below appear in the terminal (and in `renox logs` once deployed). The browser only gets `RENOX_INTERNAL` with the request id, so nothing about your schema leaks.

| You see | Why, and what to do |
| --- | --- |
| `RENOX_DB_SQL` with `no such table: app__tasks` | The migration did not run: check the file is in `migrations/` and ends in `.sql`, then save any file so `renox dev` rebuilds |
| `RENOX_DB_AUTH` | The statement touches a table without the `app__` prefix, or a module's table. Rename the table |
| `RENOX_DB_PARAM` | The number of `?` and of values differ, or a value is not a string, number, boolean, null or bytes |
| `RENOX_DB_MULTI_STATEMENT` | One `query` call holds two statements. Make two calls |
| A migration you edited does not change the table | Migrations run once. Add `002_….sql` with an `alter table` instead |

## Building with an AI agent

Ask: "Store the tasks in SQLite with a migration and read them in the loader." `AGENTS.md` tells the agent about the `app__` prefix, forward-only migrations and `?` parameters, and `run_check` catches interpolated SQL.

**Checkpoint:** [`examples/tutorial/step-04`](../../examples/tutorial/step-04/). Next: [functions and forms](05-actions.md).

---

Source: docs/tutorial/05-actions.md (https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/blob/main/docs/tutorial/05-actions.md)

# Chapter 5: Functions and forms

**What you build:** a form to add tasks, a button to tick one off and one to remove it. Each is a page **action**. With htmx, the server sends back only the task list and the page swaps it in place, without a full reload.

## Actions

A page's `.ts` file may export `actions`. A form posting to `?/add` runs `actions.add`. Each action runs in its own database transaction: it commits when the action returns and rolls back when it throws. When an action returns an object (or nothing), the page's `load` runs again and the page is rendered with that object merged over the loader's data. A `Response` is sent as it is.

`pages/board/index.ts`:
```ts
// GET /board: the tasks. POST ?/add, ?/toggle and ?/remove change them;
// an htmx request gets only the `tasks` fragment back.
import type { ActionContext, LoaderContext } from "@renoxium/sdk";

import { findTask, listTasks, parseTitle } from "../../lib/tasks";

export async function load({ db }: LoaderContext) {
  const tasks = await listTasks(db);
  return {
    tasks: tasks.map((t) => ({ ...t, done: t.done === 1 })),
    open: tasks.filter((t) => t.done === 0).length,
    error: null,
  };
}

// Each action runs in its own transaction. Returning an object (or
// nothing) runs `load` again and renders the page, or only the fragment
// htmx asked for, with that object merged over the loader's data.
export const actions = {
  async add({ db, form }: ActionContext) {
    const parsed = parseTitle(form.get("title"));
    if ("error" in parsed) return { error: parsed.error };
    await db.execute("insert into app__tasks (title, created_at) values (?, ?)", [parsed.title, Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000)]);
  },

  async toggle({ db, form }: ActionContext) {
    const task = await findTask(db, form.get("task"));
    if (task === null) return new Response("No such task", { status: 404 });
    await db.execute("update app__tasks set done = 1 - done where id = ?", [task.id]);
  },

  async remove({ db, form }: ActionContext) {
    const task = await findTask(db, form.get("task"));
    if (task === null) return new Response("No such task", { status: 404 });
    await db.execute("delete from app__tasks where id = ?", [task.id]);
  },
};
```

Three things to notice:
- **Validation first.** `parseTitle` trims the title and refuses an empty or over-long one. It returns the i18n key of the error, and the action hands it to the template as `error`.
- **The task is loaded from the database**, by its id, before it is changed. An id that does not exist is a 404, not a silent no-op.
- **Form values are strings** (or files). `form.get("task")` is turned into a number before it reaches SQL.

`lib/tasks.ts`:
```ts
export const MAX_TITLE = 200;

/** The tasks, open ones first. */
export function listTasks(db: DbStatements): Promise<Task[]> {
  return db.query<Task>("select id, title, done from app__tasks order by done, id desc limit ?", [200]);
}

/** One task, or null. */
export function findTask(db: DbStatements, id: unknown): Promise<Task | null> {
  const n = Number(id);
  if (!Number.isSafeInteger(n) || n < 1) return Promise.resolve(null);
  return db.queryOne<Task>("select id, title, done from app__tasks where id = ?", [n]);
}

/** A title as typed, or the i18n key of the reason it cannot be one. */
export function parseTitle(raw: FormDataEntryValue | null): { title: string } | { error: string } {
  const title = typeof raw === "string" ? raw.trim() : "";
  if (title === "") return { error: "board.error.empty" };
  if (title.length > MAX_TITLE) return { error: "board.error.long" };
  return { title };
}
```

## Forms with `<x-form>`

`<x-form action="add">` renders a `<form method="post" action="?/add">` with the CSRF token already inside, so the request passes the platform's CSRF check. A hand-written form needs `<x-csrf />`. The form now sits inside the `tasks` fragment:

`pages/board/index.html`:
```html
  <section id="tasks" r-fragment="tasks">
    <x-form action="add" class="add" hx-target="#tasks" hx-swap="outerHTML">
      <label><r-t key="board.new_task" /> <input name="title" maxlength="200" autocomplete="off" required></label>
      <button type="submit"><r-t key="board.add" /></button>
    </x-form>
    <p class="error" r-if="error">{{ error | t }}</p>
    <p class="count"><r-t key="board.open" :n="open | number" /></p>
    <ul>
      <li r-for="task in tasks"><x-task :task="task" /></li>
      <li class="empty" r-empty="tasks"><r-t key="board.empty" /></li>
    </ul>
  </section>
```

The partial gets the toggle and remove buttons:

`partials/task.html`:
```html
<r-props task="Task" />
<article :class="{ task: true, done: task.done }">
  <x-form action="toggle" hx-target="#tasks" hx-swap="outerHTML">
    <input type="hidden" name="task" :value="task.id">
    <button type="submit" class="check"><r-group r-if="task.done">✓</r-group><r-group r-else>○</r-group></button>
  </x-form>
  <span class="title" dir="auto">{{ task.title | truncate(80) }}</span>
  <x-form action="remove" hx-target="#tasks" hx-swap="outerHTML">
    <input type="hidden" name="task" :value="task.id">
    <button type="submit" class="remove"><r-t key="board.remove" /></button>
  </x-form>
</article>
```

`{{ error | t }}` translates the key the action returned, with the strings added to the catalogue:

`i18n/en.json`:
```json
    "new_task": "New task",
    "add": "Add",
    "remove": "Remove",
    "open": "{n} open",
    "empty": "Nothing to do yet.",
    "error": {
      "empty": "Write what needs doing.",
      "long": "Keep it under 200 characters."
```

## htmx: only the fragment

The forms work without JavaScript: the browser posts and the whole page comes back. Add htmx (one file, served from `public/`) and the same forms send `hx-post` requests instead:

`pages/_layouts/main.html`:
```html
  <meta name="htmx-config" content='{"includeIndicatorStyles": false}'>
  <title><slot name="title">Team board</slot></title>
  <link rel="stylesheet" href="/app.css">
  <script src="/htmx-2.0.4.min.js" defer></script>
```

Copy `htmx-2.0.4.min.js` from the [htmx release](https://unpkg.com/htmx.org@2.0.4/dist/htmx.min.js) (or from the checkpoint) into `public/`.

`<x-form>` already writes `hx-post`. `hx-target="#tasks"` tells htmx where the answer goes. htmx sends the target's id in the `HX-Target` header, the platform matches it to `r-fragment="tasks"`, runs the action and `load` as before, and renders only that fragment: no layout, no header, a few hundred bytes. `hx-swap="outerHTML"` replaces the old section with the new one. Because the form is inside the fragment, it comes back empty after an add.

[What you should see: one task ticked off, one open, and an empty form](screenshots/05-actions.png).

The tests drive the actions as a browser would: `t.action(path, name, form)` reads the CSRF token from a first `GET` and posts the form:

`tests/board.test.ts`:
```ts
  test("add: a task, escaped; an empty title is refused", async () => {
    const added = await t.action("/board", "add", { title: "Ship <b>it</b>" });
    expect(added.html).toContain("Ship &lt;b&gt;it&lt;/b&gt;");
    expect(added.html).toContain("3 open");
    expect((await t.action("/board", "add", { title: "   " })).html).toContain("Write what needs doing.");
  });

  test("toggle and remove", async () => {
    await t.action("/board", "toggle", { task: taskId("Invite the team") });
    expect((await t.page("/board")).html).toContain("2 open");
    await t.action("/board", "remove", { task: taskId("Ship <b>it</b>") });
    expect((await t.page("/board")).html).not.toContain("Ship &lt;b&gt;");
    expect((await t.action("/board", "toggle", { task: "999" })).status).toBe(404);
  });
```

The last test sends what htmx sends and checks that only the fragment comes back:

`tests/board.test.ts`:
```ts
  test("htmx: the fragment only, not the page", async () => {
    const res = await t.request("POST", "/board?/add", {
      headers: { "content-type": "application/x-www-form-urlencoded", "x-renox-csrf": t.cookie("__Host-renox_csrf") ?? "", "hx-request": "true", "hx-target": "tasks" },
      body: "title=Plan+the+demo",
    });
```

## If it does not work

| You see | Why, and what to do |
| --- | --- |
| `RENOX_CSRF` (403) | The form has no token: use `<x-form>`, or put `<x-csrf />` inside a hand-written form. An htmx request needs the token too; `<x-form>` covers it |
| The whole page appears inside the list | The target id and the fragment name differ. `hx-target="#tasks"` needs `r-fragment="tasks"` on the element with `id="tasks"` |
| Nothing happens on submit, and `[browser] htmx.targetError` in the terminal | The `hx-target` selector matches nothing on the page |
| "No such task" (404) | The id in the form is not a task: check the hidden input's `:value="task.id"` |
| `RENOX_DB_CONSTRAINT` | A `not null` or `check` constraint refused the row; the transaction was rolled back, so nothing half-saved |

## Building with an AI agent

Ask: "Add actions to add, toggle and remove tasks, with htmx swapping only the list." Then ask it to run the tests (`run_tests`). The `htmx: the fragment only` test is the kind of check an agent can add to prove the fragment works.

**Checkpoint:** [`examples/tutorial/step-05`](../../examples/tutorial/step-05/). Next: [sign-in and teams with modules](06-teams.md).

---

Source: docs/tutorial/06-teams.md (https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/blob/main/docs/tutorial/06-teams.md)

# Chapter 6: Sign-in and teams with modules

**What you build:** sign-up and sign-in, teams with roles, and invitations, without writing any auth code. Each task belongs to a team, and the board shows the active team's tasks.

## Install the modules

A module is a packaged piece of an app: its own tables, pages, services and policies. The official `org` module brings teams ("organisations"); it needs `auth` (users, passwords, sessions) and `i18n` (the locale). One command installs all three after showing what each asks for:

```sh
renox add org
```

```
org needs auth, which is not installed; it is installed with it:
auth 1.0.0 (official): Users, passwords (argon2id), sessions, and the login, register and account pages
It asks for:
  tables   auth__*
  network  accounts.google.com, oauth2.googleapis.com, www.googleapis.com, github.com, api.github.com, login.microsoftonline.com, graph.microsoft.com, stg-id.uaepass.ae, id.uaepass.ae
  secrets  AUTH_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET, AUTH_GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET, AUTH_MICROSOFT_CLIENT_SECRET, AUTH_UAEPASS_CLIENT_SECRET
  slots    app.header
…
Approve and install org and auth, i18n? [y/N] y
installed auth 1.0.0 (needed by org)
installed i18n 1.0.0 (needed by org)
installed org 1.0.0; run renox migrate to create its tables
```

The network hosts and secrets are for optional sign-in with Google, GitHub, Microsoft or UAE PASS. A module can reach only what you approve here, and only its own `auth__*` tables. `renox add` writes the modules into `renox.toml` and pins exact versions and content hashes in `renox.lock`:

`renox.toml`:
```toml
[modules]
org = { version = "^1.0.0" }
auth = { version = "^1.0.0" }
i18n = { version = "^1.0.0" }
outbox = { version = "^1.0.0", source = "path:modules/outbox" }
```

(`outbox` is the next section.) Save, and `renox dev` serves the modules' pages: `/auth/register`, `/auth/login`, `/auth/account`, `/org` (your teams, create one) and `/org/members` (members, roles, invitations). Roles are `member`, `admin` and `owner` ([org's README](../../modules/org/README.md)).

## Invitations need a mail sender

An admin invites by email. `org` hands the invitation to the hook `org.send_mail`, and some module must fill it. The official `email` module fills `auth.send_mail` (password resets) and, from CLI 0.1.4, `org.send_mail` too: `renox add email` delivers invitations. The board keeps `modules/outbox` so the tutorial runs without a mail provider, so it carries a ten-line module of its own. It keeps each invitation in a table so you can pass the link on yourself:

`modules/outbox/module.toml`:
```toml
[module]
name = "outbox"
version = "1.0.0"
description = "Keeps the invitation mails org asks to send, so a team can be tried before a mail module delivers them"

[permissions]
tables = "outbox__*"
hooks = ["org.send_mail"]
```

`modules/outbox/hooks.ts`:
```ts
// org asks `org.send_mail` to deliver an invitation; no official module
// sends it yet, so this one keeps the mail in outbox__mail for the
// owner to pass on. Replace it with a mail module before real users join.
interface Mail {
  to: string;
  template: string;
  args: { url: string; org_name: string };
}

interface HookCtx {
  db: { execute(sql: string, params?: unknown[]): Promise<unknown> };
}

export const hooks = {
  "org.send_mail": {
    async handle(ctx: HookCtx, mail: Mail) {
      await ctx.db.execute("insert into outbox__mail (mail_to, template, url, org_name, created_at) values (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [mail.to, mail.template, mail.args.url, mail.args.org_name, Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000)]);
    },
  },
};
```

`modules/outbox/migrations/001_init.sql`:
```sql
create table outbox__mail (
  id         integer primary key,
  mail_to    text    not null,
  template   text    not null,
  url        text    not null,
  org_name   text    not null,
  created_at integer not null
) strict;
```

```sh
renox add outbox --source path:modules/outbox
```

Replace it with a mail module before real users join. Until then, the link of an invitation is in `outbox__mail.url`.

## A task belongs to a team

Migrations only move forward, so the team goes into a new file:

`migrations/002_tasks_team.sql`:
```sql
-- Chapter 6: a task belongs to a team. Migrations only move forward, so
-- the column is added here, not written into 001.
alter table app__tasks add column team_id text not null default '';
create index app__tasks_team on app__tasks (team_id, id);
```

Every query now names the team. A task of another team is never read or changed, because the `where` clause says so:

`lib/tasks.ts`:
```ts
export function listTasks(db: DbStatements, team: string): Promise<Task[]> {
  return db.query<Task>("select id, title, done, team_id from app__tasks where team_id = ? order by done, id desc limit 200", [team]);
}

/** One task of the team, or null. */
export function findTask(db: DbStatements, team: string, id: unknown): Promise<Task | null> {
  const n = Number(id);
  if (!Number.isSafeInteger(n) || n < 1) return Promise.resolve(null);
  return db.queryOne<Task>("select id, title, done, team_id from app__tasks where id = ? and team_id = ?", [n, team]);
}
```

The loader asks `org` for the active team. A module's services are imported from `renox:modules`; the call runs as the signed-in user, so `currentOrg()` is that user's active team or `null`:

`pages/board/index.ts`:
```ts
export async function load({ db, url }: LoaderContext) {
  // The header's slot renders auth's user menu (auth_user) and org's team switcher (org_switcher).
  const auth_user = await auth.currentUser();
  const org_switcher = await org.switcher(url.pathname);
  const team = await org.currentOrg();
  if (team === null) return { auth_user, org_switcher, team: null, tasks: [], open: 0, error: null };
  const tasks = await listTasks(db, team.id);
  return {
    auth_user,
    org_switcher,
    team: { name: team.name },
    tasks: tasks.map((t) => ({ ...t, done: t.done === 1 })),
    open: tasks.filter((t) => t.done === 0).length,
    error: null,
  };
}

/** The active team, or a Response that ends the action. */
async function activeTeam(): Promise<{ id: string; role: string } | Response> {
  const team = await org.currentOrg();
  return team ?? new Response("Sign in and create a team first", { status: 409 });
}
```

The actions use `activeTeam()` and pass `team.id` to every query. The template shows a link to `/org` when there is no team yet:

`pages/board/index.html`:
```html
  <r-group r-if="!team">
    <p><r-t key="board.no_team" /> <a href="/org"><r-t key="board.create_team" /></a></p>
  </r-group>
  <r-group r-else>
    <p class="team">{{ team.name | upper }}</p>
```

The layout gets the modules' header: `<r-slot name="app.header" />` is filled by `auth` (the user menu, from `auth_user`) and `org` (the team switcher, from `org_switcher`):

`pages/_layouts/main.html`:
```html
  <header>
    <a href="/"><strong>Team board</strong></a>
    <a href="/board"><r-t key="board.title" /></a>
    <r-slot name="app.header" />
  </header>
```

## Types for `renox:modules`

`renox check` type checks your calls to `org`, but it does not see the module types `renox dev` generates under `.renox/types/` (#471). Until it does, declare what you call:

`renox-modules.d.ts`:
```ts
// The services of `renox:modules` this app calls. The type check needs
// this file until the generated module types are picked up (chapter 6).
declare module "renox:modules" {
  export const auth: {
    currentUser(): Promise<{ id: string; email: string; display_name: string } | null>;
  };
  export const org: {
    currentOrg(): Promise<{ id: string; slug: string; name: string; role: string } | null>;
    switcher(next?: string): Promise<unknown>;
  };
}
```

## The sample rows go

`seeds/tasks.sql` is gone in this step: its rows would belong to no team, and no one would see them.

## See it

Register at http://localhost:8787/auth/register, create a team at `/org`, then open `/board`. [What you should see: the team name, the user menu and the team switcher](screenshots/06-team.png).

The tests sign users up through the real `auth` pages and check that teams are kept apart:

`tests/board.test.ts`:
```ts
describe("the board, per team", () => {
  test("a new user creates a team, then adds and ticks off its tasks", async () => {
    const lina = await signUp("Lina");
    expect((await lina.page("/board")).html).toContain("You are not in a team yet.");
    expect((await lina.action("/org", "create", { name: "Acme" })).status).toBe(303);
    await lina.action("/board", "add", { title: "Write the tutorial" });
    await lina.action("/board", "toggle", { task: taskId("Write the tutorial") });
    const page = await lina.page("/board");
    expect(page.html).toContain("ACME");
    expect(page.html).toContain('<article class="task done">');
  });

  test("another team sees none of it and cannot change it", async () => {
    const sara = await signUp("Sara");
    await sara.action("/org", "create", { name: "Other" });
    expect((await sara.page("/board")).html).not.toContain("Write the tutorial");
    expect((await sara.action("/board", "toggle", { task: taskId("Write the tutorial") })).status).toBe(404);
  });
});
```

## If it does not work

| You see | Why, and what to do |
| --- | --- |
| `TS2307: Cannot find module 'renox:modules'` | Add `renox-modules.d.ts` as above (#471) |
| "Sign in and create a team first" (409) | The session has no active team: create one at `/org` |
| `RENOX_MODULE_SERVICE` in the terminal | A module's service threw (for example `org` refused a call the user's role does not allow). The module's own log line, just above, names the cause |
| `renox add` reports `MF2` or `MF11` | The version range in `renox.toml` cannot be met, or the module's source cannot be read. For a `path:` module, the folder must hold `module.toml` |
| An invitation never arrives | The board fills `org.send_mail` with `modules/outbox`, which delivers nothing; read the link from `outbox__mail`. From CLI 0.1.4, `renox add email` delivers invitations too |
| `MF12: outbox.hash in renox.lock is "…", expected "…"` after you edit `modules/outbox` | The lock pins the module's content hash. Run `renox add outbox --source path:modules/outbox` again |

## Building with an AI agent

Ask: "Add sign-in and teams with the official modules; each task belongs to the active team." The agent should call `renox add` and not write auth code: `AGENTS.md` says so. Check that it scoped every query to the team; the tests above are the proof.

**Checkpoint:** [`examples/tutorial/step-06`](../../examples/tutorial/step-06/). Next: [authorization](07-authorization.md).

Source: docs/tutorial/07-authorization.md (https://github.com/arif-rachim/renox.rs/blob/main/docs/tutorial/07-authorization.md)

# Chapter 7: Authorization

**What you build:** a Cedar policy that says who may open the board and who may change a team's tasks; a guard on the page; checks in the actions on the task as stored; and remove buttons only for admins and owners.

Chapter 6 already filters every query by team. This chapter states the rule once, as a policy, so the page, the actions, the template and later the live feed all ask the same question.

## Declare the actions

`renox.toml`:
```toml
# Chapter 7: who may do what on the board (policies/app/board.cedar).
[authz]
actions = ["board.view", "task.edit", "task.delete"]

[authz.entities]
Task = { table = "app__tasks", attrs = ["team_id"] }
```

`actions` are the names your policies and code use. `[authz.entities]` declares `Task` as a resource type with the attribute `team_id`, so a policy can compare it.

## The policy

Policies live in `policies/app/*.cedar` ([Cedar](https://www.cedarpolicy.com) is a policy language from AWS; Renoxium evaluates it in Rust):

`policies/app/board.cedar`:
```cedar
// Chapter 7: the board's policies. `principal.org` is the session's active
// team; the org module puts it on the principal.

// The page's guard: any signed-in user opens /board.
permit (principal is Renox::User, action == Renox::Action::"board.view", resource == Renox::Action::"board.view");

// Members of the team add and tick off its tasks, and nobody else.
permit (principal is Renox::User, action == Renox::Action::"task.edit", resource is App::Task)
when { principal has org && resource.team_id == principal.org };

// Removing is for the team too; the action also asks for an admin or an
// owner (chapter 7 explains why that check is not here).
permit (principal is Renox::User, action == Renox::Action::"task.delete", resource is App::Task)
when { principal has org && resource.team_id == principal.org };
```

`principal.org` is the session's active team. The `org` module puts it on the principal, so a policy can compare it with `resource.team_id`. Nothing is allowed unless a `permit` matches: a missing attribute, an unknown action or a visitor who is not signed in all mean deny.

## Use it

**The guard** runs before any code of the page. A visitor who is not signed in gets 403 (`RENOX_FORBIDDEN`) and the loader never runs:

`pages/board/index.ts`:
```ts
/** Signed-in users only: checked before any code of this page runs. */
export const guard = { action: "board.view" };
```

**In the actions**, `authz.require` checks the task as loaded from the database, never as the form describes it, and throws `RENOX_FORBIDDEN` (403) on a deny:

`pages/board/index.ts`:
```ts
  async toggle({ db, form, authz }: ActionContext) {
    const team = await activeTeam();
    if (team instanceof Response) return team;
    const task = await findTask(db, team.id, form.get("task"));
    if (task === null) return new Response("No such task", { status: 404 });
    // The task as loaded from the database, never as the form describes it.
    await authz.require("task.edit", asResource(task));
    await db.execute("update app__tasks set done = 1 - done where id = ?", [task.id]);
  },
```

`asResource` turns a row into what the policy sees:

`lib/tasks.ts`:
```ts
/** A task as the policy sees it: its type, id and the attributes renox.toml declares. */
export const asResource = (t: Task) => ({ type: "Task", id: String(t.id), team_id: t.team_id });
```

## Only admins and owners remove

The natural policy for that is `permit (principal in Renox::Role::"admin", …)`. Today it would never match: `org` keeps a member's role in its own table and does not hand it to the policy engine as a role assignment (#470). So the policy allows removing for the team, and the action adds the role check, with the role from `org.currentOrg()`:

`pages/board/index.ts`:
```ts
  async remove({ db, form, authz }: ActionContext) {
    const team = await activeTeam();
    if (team instanceof Response) return team;
    const task = await findTask(db, team.id, form.get("task"));
    if (task === null) return new Response("No such task", { status: 404 });
    await authz.require("task.delete", asResource(task));
    // Only the team's admins and owners (chapter 7 says why this is not in the policy).
    if (team.role === "member") return new Response("Only admins and owners remove tasks", { status: 403 });
    await db.execute("delete from app__tasks where id = ?", [task.id]);
  },
```

The template hides the button the same way. `r-can="task.delete" :resource="task"` asks the policy for each task, and `manager` carries the role:

`partials/task.html`:
```html
  <x-form action="remove" hx-target="#tasks" hx-swap="outerHTML" r-if="manager" r-can="task.delete" :resource="task">
    <input type="hidden" name="task" :value="task.id">
    <button type="submit" class="remove"><r-t key="board.remove" /></button>
  </x-form>
```

Hiding a button is a convenience, not protection: the action checks again, and a hand-made `POST` without the role gets 403. The loader computes `manager` once:

`pages/board/index.ts`:
```ts
    // Admins and owners see the remove buttons; the action checks it again.
    team: { name: team.name, manager: team.role !== "member" },
```

## Test the policy

`policies/tests/*.json` cases are evaluated by `renox test` with the same engine, without a browser or a database:

`policies/tests/board.json`:
```json
[
  { "description": "a signed-in user opens the board", "principal": { "type": "User", "id": "u_lina" }, "action": "board.view", "expected": "allow" },
  { "description": "a visitor who is not signed in does not", "principal": { "type": "Anonymous", "id": "anonymous" }, "action": "board.view", "expected": "deny" },
  { "description": "a member ticks off a task of their team", "principal": { "type": "User", "id": "u_omar", "attrs": { "org": "o_acme" } }, "action": "task.edit", "resource": { "type": "Task", "id": "1", "team_id": "o_acme" }, "expected": "allow" },
  { "description": "not a task of another team", "principal": { "type": "User", "id": "u_omar", "attrs": { "org": "o_acme" } }, "action": "task.edit", "resource": { "type": "Task", "id": "2", "team_id": "o_other" }, "expected": "deny" },
  { "description": "nor without a team", "principal": { "type": "User", "id": "u_sara" }, "action": "task.edit", "resource": { "type": "Task", "id": "1", "team_id": "o_acme" }, "expected": "deny" },
  { "description": "a task of the team may be removed", "principal": { "type": "User", "id": "u_lina", "attrs": { "org": "o_acme" } }, "action": "task.delete", "resource": { "type": "Task", "id": "1", "team_id": "o_acme" }, "expected": "allow" },
  { "description": "not one of another team", "principal": { "type": "User", "id": "u_sara", "attrs": { "org": "o_other" } }, "action": "task.delete", "resource": { "type": "Task", "id": "1", "team_id": "o_acme" }, "expected": "deny" }
]
```

```
(pass) policy policies/tests/board.json: a member ticks off a task of their team -> allow
(pass) policy policies/tests/board.json: not a task of another team -> deny
…
```

`renox authz explain --user <id> --action task.edit --resource Task:1` prints which policy decided a request on the dev database. It does not run the `org` hook, so give the attribute yourself: `--attr org=o_acme` sets `principal.org`. The output lists the attributes it used.

## See it

Invite a second user from `/org/members` (the link is in `outbox__mail`), accept it in another browser, and open `/board` as them. [What you should see: the member's board, without remove buttons](screenshots/07-member.png).

## If it does not work

| You see | Why, and what to do |
| --- | --- |
| 403 `RENOX_FORBIDDEN` on `/board` when signed in | No `permit` matches `board.view`. Check the action name in `renox.toml`, the policy and the guard are the same |
| `RENOX_POLICY_INVALID` from `renox check` | The policy names an action or entity that is not declared, or an attribute with the wrong type. The message names the file and line |
| `RENOX_FORBIDDEN` with `reason: missing_attribute` in the log | The resource object lacks `team_id`: pass `asResource(task)`, not the raw form values |
| Every request is denied for a team member | `principal.org` is missing: the user has no active team (create or switch at `/org`) |
| An owner cannot remove | Check `team.role`; `org` roles are `member`, `admin` and `owner` |

## Building with an AI agent

Ask: "Write a Cedar policy so only members of the active team can change its tasks, with policy tests." The agent has `list_policies` and `authz_explain` over MCP; with the gap above, have it prove the policy with `policies/tests/*.json` cases and `run_tests`.

**Checkpoint:** [`examples/tutorial/step-07`](../../examples/tutorial/step-07/). Next: [realtime](08-realtime.md).
